Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

📅 09 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, ah, creatine!
  • Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Industry observers note that although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Industry observers note that although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

It has been revealed that now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a major-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

It has been revealed that so, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

Industry observers note that the same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Recent findings suggest that does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

Industry observers note that if you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health challenges that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

Assemble covers miniature agricultural buildings in intense blue pigment for Building Blue exhibition in Tokyo

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a new pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.
  • With the exhibition, the UK-based collective remarked it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.
  • The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the upcoming pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a new pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective remarked it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.

The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the upcoming pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.

The blue hue was manufactured by Japanese company Nikken to be used in the Play Earth Park – a campsite designed by Assemble that is presently under development in rural Japan.

“The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them,” Matter at hand founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

“In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC,” he continued.

“The materials react to form a upcoming crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue.”.

To show it off, Assemble constructed three miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced. The houses were named The Hut, The Tower and The Bird.

“The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries,” Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

“We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play.”.

The buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.

Assemble’s aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.

“We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT,” Lisogorskaya noted.

“The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn’t expect.”.

The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC’s) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.

Assemble said it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.

“We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool,” Lisogorskaya said.

“Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city,” she continued.

SKAC recently opened two new gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.

The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.

Building Blue is at SKAC, 3-26-4 Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo 125-0002, from 7 November 2026 to 28 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

📅 26 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing.
  • It has been revealed that wondering how to tell the difference?
  • Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

It has been revealed that wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:.

According to recent reports, caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Sources indicate that chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner aims suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future aims feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

Recent findings suggest that if imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love intends a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Recent findings suggest that remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

In a recent development, shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears.
  • Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort.
  • Sources indicate that clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home. Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up! Why are my ears clogged? Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked: Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage. If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection. Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side. Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too. Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure. Best clogged ear remedies 1. Pop and unclog The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes. 2. Swallow, yawn, or chew The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow. 3. Ear drops Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes. Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful. 4. Warmth and gravity To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily. 5. Hit the steam room Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 6. Take allergy medication Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears. Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort. 7. Rinse away the gunk Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing. When to see your doctor Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention. What not to do when you have clogged ears Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries. Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion. Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation. Takeaway Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies. PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

According to recent reports, if you've been waiting for the right 3D printer deal to start exploring this exciting craft, Black Friday is your moment. The Elegoo Black Friday sale is in full swing, and the Centauri Carbon 2 Combo, a machine we highly recommend for beginners, is reduced by $80 to $369 at Amazon.

We think this is an ideal choice for beginners since it's easy to set up and run, offers good value and provides plenty of flexibility to grow as a creator since it can handle a range of materials and multi-colour printing (see our guide to the best 3D printers to see how it compares to other options we've tested). There are also a couple of great deals running on Elegoo resin printers if you want to make more detailed objects, and the brand's running discounts on resins and filaments.

According to recent reports, hitting the sweet spot for speed, quality and versatility at an accessible price, the Centauri Carbon 2 Combo FDM printer is suitable for everyone from first-time makers to experienced creators. The enclosed CoreXY design, automated setup and leveling, intuitive user interface, 350°C hardened-steel nozzle and four-colour system offer an approachable path into multicolour printing while providing the performance and flexibility to push projects.

The open-frame Centauri 2 is reduced to $279 but the Carbon version's closed frame has the benefit of allowing the use of temperature-sensitive materials such as ABS, ASA, nylon, polycarbonate and carbon fiber filaments.

It has been revealed that the Saturn 4 is a resin printer for creators who need precise, ultra-fine detail with high surface quality. With a 16K LCD, it offers large build volume, a heated vat, and automatic levelling and tilt-release technology for an efficient workflow ideal for tabletop gaming models, miniatures and collectible characters.

See our full Elegoo Saturn 4 Ultra review.

For a more economical introduction to resin 3D printing, the Mars 5 Ultra is an accessible option for tabletop gamers and miniature enthusiasts. Automatic leveling, tilt release and print-failure detection keep the setup and operation simple, while 9K resolution can deliver detailed results if not as fine as the 16K Saturn 4 Ultra above.

It has been revealed that for most beginners, an FDM (fused deposition modeling) 3D printer is the way to go. They're safer, cleaner, cheaper to run, and easier to post-process than resin printers. We recommend the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 Combo because as well as making things as easy as possible, it provides plenty of versatility to dive deep once you're ready to start getting more hands on and to develop in 3D printing, without having to go out an buy another machine that allows more flexibility.

It leaves very little work to do in assembly, with no gantries to bolt together. You just remove the accessories and shipping foam, plug in the screen, and you can be up and running in a few minutes. It offers a practical mid-size build volume of 256 × 256 × 256mm (10.1 × 10.1 × 10.1 inches), the closed frame means you can work with a wide range of materials and there's the option of multi-colour printing.

There's also a built-in camera, so you can film timelapses of your print jobs and monitor in real time, and it has a self-clean function.

In a recent development, my exception to this recommendation would be if you specifically want to create detailed miniatures or character models, which require ultra-fine precision and a higher surface quality. For that, the best-value introduction is the Mars 5 Ultra.

Industry observers note that tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

According to recent reports, tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

In a recent development, want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

According to recent reports, tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Sources indicate that are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s upcoming best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

According to recent reports, fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

In a recent development, tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Recent findings suggest that flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over one hundred staff at Edinburgh College of Art have signed an open letter addressed to the university, calling on the institution to reverse its decision to cut three craft-focussed design courses from its programme.
  • The open letter was signed by 109 unnamed staff members of Edinburgh College of Art (ECA), which confirmed on 15 September that it would stop admitting students for its undergraduate courses in jewellery and silversmithing, textiles and performance costume from 2027.
  • The move is part of a wider decision by the University of Edinburgh, which the art college merged with in 2011, to make £140 million’s worth of cuts to arts and humanities courses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photo by Colin Hattersley.

Over one hundred staff at Edinburgh College of Art have signed an open letter addressed to the university, calling on the institution to reverse its decision to cut three craft-focussed design courses from its programme.

Open letter states “deep concern”.

The open letter was signed by 109 unnamed staff members of Edinburgh College of Art (ECA), which confirmed on 15 September that it would stop admitting students for its undergraduate courses in jewellery and silversmithing, textiles and performance costume from 2027.

The move is part of a wider decision by the University of Edinburgh, which the art college merged with in 2011, to make £140 million’s worth of cuts to arts and humanities courses.

“We the undersigned are writing to mark our deep concern about the University of Edinburgh’s current financially-driven restructuring,” states the letter, which was written by an unnamed senior lecturer in the school of design and published yesterday.

“As staff who collectively provide and deliver the teaching, research, technical expertise and administration of design, we assert that there is irreparable harm being done to the core values of our subject area, school, and to the art, craft and design professions in Scotland at large,” it continues.

The open letter also asks the university to retract its decision to close the courses and requests better communication between the university and its employees.

Signatories describe an “alienating” period during which the decision to close the courses was “made without prior consultation with [the university] staff”.

“Rash decision-making based on unsubstantiated and opaque data seems to be characterising the announcements of closures and cuts, and there has been no dialogue with students and staff that can be understood as meaningful or considered consultation,” they state.

“We feel that the area’s staff have been treated callously or with very little regard by senior management, and we are writing, in part, to warn you of the damage this has created and ask you to make effort to repair it.”.

Courses part of “wider ecosystem”.

The letter goes on to emphasise the importance of “individual programmes as valuable parts of [a] wider ecosystem”, and particularly stresses the urgency of craft-based undergraduate courses in the creative sphere.

“Looking specifically at jewellery and silversmithing, textiles, and performance costume, these are subjects that teach, in different and inherently valuable ways, specialised material knowledge and sensibilities, innovative critiques, and developments of systems of production and consumption, great capacities to research-through-making, and the ability to speak to a society’s needs through aesthetic form, the power of narrative, and the arts of material, chemical and technological mastery and manipulation,” it states.

The letter is addressed to the University of Edinburgh Court, the university’s governing body, which is scheduled to meet on 7 December to review the decision.

Industry observers note that the open letter is the most recent statement issued by a collective against the decision to cut the courses. It follows a live petition led by arts organisation Craft Scotland calling for the urgent reinstatement of “the only undergraduate craft courses offered by Edinburgh College of Art” amidst public backlash.

In response to the letter, ECA principal Juan Cruz commented, “we remain committed to the strength and distinctiveness of our disciplines, as well as to the many other making and craft-based approaches that we offer at Edinburgh College of Art”.

“These subjects will continue to be represented within the wider curriculum, supported by ECA’s specialist academic and technical expertise and facilities,” he added.

Photo by Colin Hattersley.

That's just one publication, but the news has made a massive impact, and the significance is clear: users may not be 100% sure when they are or aren't using generative AI to edit an image.

There's an easy solution, but will Adobe want to introduce it?

The Upcoming York Times wrote in an email to freelance photographers that the newest version of Photoshop “utilizes generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to people. Their use can result in metadata misidentifying photos as AI-generated.” As a result photographers have been told not to use the latest version of the software.

In photojournalism, it's an ethical problem. Images need to reflect reality, so editing is usually relatively limited. The inadvertent use of generative AI also brings with it the risk of an "AI content" tag on social media, which could lead people to question a report, and could severely damage to the reputation of both the photographer and any media outlet reporting news with an image flagged as AI.

Recent findings suggest that the most obvious solution would be an AI-off switch. Digital artists, designers and those photographers who want to use generative AI tools in Photoshop could turn it on. Photojournalists, documentary photographers, and anyone who simply doesn't want to use generative AI or risk being shamed with an AI content tag, can turn it off.

Industry observers note that other software developers have done just that. Canva added an AI off Switch last week, and Maxon has included the ability to turn off its latest generative AI features in Cinema 4D and ZBrush. It's a simple mechanism that can be flicked on or off at any time, and the gesture helps offer reassurance to those owners who oppose AI.

The question is whether Adobe will be willing to follow this lead, or if it will fear that a switch would call its direction into question or discourage people from using the AI tools it wants to promote.

Adobe didn't immediately respond to an invitation to comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

According to recent reports, each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

It has been revealed that from those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:.

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Industry observers note that lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of fresh love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Industry observers note that hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the problems head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

In a recent development, significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

Industry observers note that you know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

  • Sources indicate that the original Grand Theft Auto logo created by The Designers Republic for the first game's marketing featured cartoonish stars and flames for a '70s vibe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if you haven't spent every waking hour of the past seven days immersed in the world of Leonida, you've sure seen a lot of the GTA logo lately. Along with the Vice City palette of pastel pinks, blues and sunset oranges, the logo has been everywhere, from developer Rockstar Games' billboards and murals to those GTA VI brand reactions.

It has been revealed that for long-time fans of series, the GTA VI logo is a familiar design with the same core wordmark that's been in use since Grand Theft Auto III. But older readers who have never played GTA might also find it strangely familiar. That could be because it's based on a free typeface that was inspired by a very different kind of game.

Sources indicate that the original Grand Theft Auto logo created by The Designers Republic for the first game's marketing featured cartoonish stars and flames for a '70s vibe. It was replaced by a simpler three-letter GTA logo for the second game, in the franchise. It was Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 that introduced the design we know today.

According to recent reports, the logo is largely based on Pricedown, a free typeface developed by the Canadian designer Raymond Larabie and published by Typodermic. In his post about the history of the font on the foundry's website, Raymond claims his intention was to closely reinterpret Pinto Flare, a display face made for Franklin Photolettering in the late 1960s and best known for its use in The Price Is Right logo.

"I kept the boxy structure and the odd unicase letterforms with swash descenders, but I drew my version harder and more angular compared to Pinto Flare’s softer feel," he writes.

Raymond notes he released Pricedown on 30 November 1997. That was just two days after the first GTA came out for windows. And the coincidences don't end there. He says that when the font was later chosen by Rockstar's office in New York, he happened to be working as an art director at Rockstar Toronto. His colleagues weren't aware that someone working at the company had designed the font.

It has been revealed that so the world's most expensive video game has a logo based on a free font? And it works: the chunky letterforms with their rounded corners work perfectly achieving easy readability while fitting into the rest of the game's branding.

In a recent development, but it would be a simplification to say that Pricedown is all there is to the GTA logo. Ultimately, Rockstar modified the letterforms and arranged them to make them work as a logo design. The three words of the franchise's name and held tightly in a block that's almost square, the 'r' and 'h' conjoin, and a black stroke provides separation against coloured backgrounds.

An additional touch has been added for each game in the form of the numbering: a pink neon sign-like script for Vice City, tattoo-like blackletter type for San Andreas, the V that recalls US currency design for GTA V.

Considering Grand Theft Auto's satire of US culture and society, it seems fitting for it to have a logo inspired by the identity of one of the country's longest-running TV series (see our pick of the best GTA VI Easter eggs for examples of how the game references pop culture and its own legacy).

Looking for the font? The original Pricedown, now called Pricedown Black is available free for desktop use, and you can download it directly from Typodermic. Raymond later expanded the font into a complete typeface family with other weights. To use those, you'll need to buy a licence. You can find them at MyFonts.

For more on the game of the biggest video game in history, check out our interviews with Rockstar Games' art team on GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:.

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he notes.

Sources indicate that as Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

It has been revealed that “Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe states. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”.

It has been revealed that nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he states.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe indicates.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

#138378. Tech Report: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1732 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1732 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from New York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.
  • It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including BIG, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.
  • Sources indicate that and yet, not everyone is a fan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Main photo by Dimitar Harizanov.

For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from New York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.

It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including BIG, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

Sources indicate that and yet, not everyone is a fan. Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.

It has been revealed that so, are the haters right on this one? Or do the arguments stack up in favour of wooded buildings?

To proponents of the approach, some of the benefits of putting trees on buildings are indisputable.

Industry observers note that “I’m totally in favor of not only trees on buildings, but any type of natural habitats on buildings wherever it’s possible,” mentioned Fernando Scherner, an associate director in the nature and biodiversity team at engineering firm Buro Happold. “There are a few things that I think we can’t even argue about anymore.”.

Sources indicate that there is, Scherner told Dezeen, strong evidence that vegetation on buildings bolsters biodiversity. And, he says, “there’s no discussion” that done right, shade and evapotranspiration from leaves can effectively keep homes cooler in hot weather, reducing the need for air conditioning – and therefore energy use.

But this second point gestures towards the crux of the debate about trees on buildings.

Industry observers note that such buildings require extra structural material to support the weight of the trees and soil, increasing the carbon cost by more than what the trees themselves will be able to sequester. Critics therefore argue that any carbon savings from reduced energy use are a red herring, because a similar benefit could be achieved through much simpler passive cooling measures such as awnings and shutters.

“I think that criticism is entirely legitimate, particularly if carbon sequestration is being used as the main justification,” said World Green Building Council technical lead for sustainable buildings Carolina Montano Owen.

“Trees do sequester carbon, but relatively slowly compared with the upfront emissions that can arise from additional reinforced concrete or steel needed for large planters, supporting structure and associated systems.”.

Sources indicate that even Dutch architecture studio MVRDV, one of the most fervent incorporators of trees on buildings, admitted in its Carbon Confessions exhibition held earlier this year that it would take hundreds of years to offset the climate impact of its La Serre project in Paris, at the moment under construction. MVRDV declined to contribute to this article.

While the phenomenon of trees on buildings goes back hundreds of years, to the Guinigi Tower in Tuscany, the undisputed poster child for the current movement stands at the other end of Italy.

Sources indicate that bosco Verticale in Milan is a pair of residential high-rises covered in 21,000 plants, including 800 trees up to 20 metres tall. It caused a sensation upon its completion in 2014, and was later selected by Dezeen as that year’s most significant building in the world.

The architect behind Bosco Verticale, Stefano Boeri, has since delivered other “vertical forests” in Eindhoven, Huanggang, Tirana and Utrecht, with several more on the way.

According to recent reports, as you’d expect, he is bullish about the benefits of putting trees on buildings. He points to analysis by Arup, which concluded that the embodied carbon of Bosco Verticale is just one per cent greater than a comparable building with balconies of the same depth without vegetation.

“The load of the greenery, including the soil, trees and so on, really only slightly exceeds the variable loads that, in any case, must necessarily be taken into account in the structural design of cantilevered space,” he told Dezeen.

Boeri argues that changes to the construction process – such as the use of prefabrication methods or mass timber – promise to cut the embodied cost further in future vertical forest projects.

Even so, Philip Oldfield, head of the University of Newly introduced South Wales’ School of Built Environment, is not convinced.

“I think the equation is pretty challenging to make the case that trees on buildings are beneficial from a greenhouse-gas emissions perspective,” he told Dezeen.

However, Oldfield points out, that’s not to say that architects adorning their buildings with trees are necessarily acting in bad faith.

It has been revealed that “I’m a fan of Bosco Verticale,” he noted. “I think it’s a really inspiring building, but not from a carbon perspective.”.

“What inspires me about Bosco Verticale is it says, ‘hey, look: you can have a hint of suburban lifestyle in a high-rise urban building,’ which could make high-density living more attractive to a greater socio-economic spectrum, and then that may be more sustainable in the long run.”.

Though harder to measure than carbon, it’s generally acknowledged that incorporating greenery into dense urban settings has positives for human wellbeing.

For instance, when Oldfield helped to conduct a post-occupancy study of the social housing development Pinnacle@Duxton in Singapore, he witnessed children sitting under trees to do their homework 50 storeys in the sky.

“Singapore’s been able to add trees and green across its built environment, and it has fundamentally changed the experience of the city, I think for the better,” he said.

With a very high-rise urban landscape, year-round hot weather, lots of rain and low wind speeds, Singapore is the perfect setting for buildings bearing trees, and the construction industry here has become adept at making it work.

In a recent development, but in other parts of the world, things have gone less successfully. Jean Nouvel’s One Central Park in Sydney, for example, had to undergo emergency repairs after one of its heavy planter boxes fell to the ground in 2022.

And in Chengdu, there were reports that barely any of the 826 apartments at Qiyi City Forest Garden were occupied a few years after its completion due to a mosquito infestation.

Even the most ardent fans of trees on buildings agree that it’s not always the right solution.

Sources indicate that “I’m totally positive about it, but I think it should be taken case-by-case,” said Scherner. “There may be cases where the purpose or the objective of the project are not really realistic.”.

“If the right multidisciplinary team is not there from the start – and I’m talking about ecologists, horticulturalists, together with engineers, structural engineers, architects, landscape architects and all that – then many things can go wrong.”.

“There are many flops,” stated Boeri. “If you decide to follow the approach that we have, you take several risks, so it’s very notable to be aware of the risk and to run all the technical problems and tools that you need if you want to do it properly.”.

“Botany is not a superficial discipline – it’s very complex, very rich, and so when you want to realise a building where trees are acting as live subjects, you have to study a lot.”.

Bosco Verticale was subject to a huge amount of strategic planning in collaboration with botanists, from the selection and preparation of the plants, to soil chemistry, to developing systems for irrigation and maintenance.

In a recent development, “Flying gardeners” now scale the buildings twice a year, while thousands of ladybirds were purchased to control pests and cranes were installed on top of the towers in anticipation of removing larger dead trees. In the event, Boeri claims fewer than 15 trees have died at Bosco Verticale, and the cranes have never been required.

Sceptics’ early predictions of mass plant deaths at buildings bearing trees have, in general, not come to pass.

But concern about whether some of these buildings are more interested in making a visual statement than being ecologically responsible has lingered.

For Montano Owen, this is the crucial test of whether the approach is justified.

“The difference is whether planting is an integrated environmental strategy or primarily aesthetic,” she said.

“A poor example is essentially decorative: oversized concrete or steel planters added to achieve a ‘green’ aesthetic, substantial additional structural loads, high irrigation requirements, inappropriate species, difficult maintenance access and high tree mortality.”.

Boeri agrees. “I believe that what we have done works because we were not considering plants as an ornamental presence, and this is very important for me,” he stated. “What we are doing is really to create buildings for trees, a house for trees.”.

Among the most high-profile projects accused of using trees as mere decoration is Heatherwick Studio’s 1,000 Trees shopping centre in Shanghai, completed in 2022.

Soon after the finished building was unveiled, Oldfield criticised the design in a piece on Dezeen.

“The trees are a one-liner, contributing to a sense of urban drama, but with little substance as to how they might provide tangible benefits to the environment, or the community,” he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that subject to similar criticisms recently was MVRDV’s design for the upcoming Rotterdam Rocks!. Writing on Dezeen, architecture historian Barnabas Calder called for the project to be scrapped, saying that “putting plants on a building doesn’t make it sustainable, any more than dropping a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan”.

These studios may argue – as Heatherwick Studio leader Thomas Heatherwick has previously done – that there is intrinsic value in designing buildings that capture the imagination of the public.

That in turn feeds into a broader debate about whether the priority for architecture should be to minimise up-front carbon, or maximise the chance that buildings are retained by future generations.

In any case, with the trees-on-buildings trend showing little sign of abating, Montano Owen has a checklist for architects taking up the approach.

“Start with the local context and environmental needs,” she mentioned. “Choose species that are suited to the location. Minimise extra structure, materials and loads. Consider water and maintenance needs from the start. Plan for vegetation to survive, grow and mature long term. Avoid solutions that need heavy structures, intensive irrigation or frequent plant replacement for limited environmental benefit.”.

Industry observers note that “The key question is this,” she added. “Is this the best place and most resource-efficient way to achieve the environmental benefits we want? Sometimes trees on buildings could make sense. In most cases, trees at street or ground level may provide greater benefits with fewer resources.”.

#138376. What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1177 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one glitch keeps coming up: the side effects.
  • To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet.
  • In a recent development, but if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one glitch keeps coming up: the side effects. As important as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

In a recent development, but if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she indicates. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”.

Fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen notes.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen notes. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

According to recent reports, fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing issue worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen says: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Recent findings suggest that now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation problem), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen says.

With that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen claims. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

Recent findings suggest that people who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we said above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen says. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”.

Industry observers note that another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

Whatever new fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu states. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

📅 30 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets.
  • Sources indicate that protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant!
  • And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Sources indicate that protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Sources indicate that farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Recent findings suggest that some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are significant, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:.

In a recent development, don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Industry observers note that sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

In a recent development, what you blend your protein powder with can make a massive difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Adobe isn’t "just ticking a box" – how diversity is shaping its products

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I recently had the privilege of attending this year's Adobe MAX, and amidst the flurry of excitement and innovations, what surprised me was the sense of community.
  • In a recent development, the phrase "finding your tribe" was thrown around profusely during the conference, and while I find the term mildly ickworthy, it bears truth.
  • It's no secret the creative industry was, and at times still is, a place of inequality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I recently had the privilege of attending this year's Adobe MAX, and amidst the flurry of excitement and innovations, what surprised me was the sense of community.

In a recent development, the phrase "finding your tribe" was thrown around profusely during the conference, and while I find the term mildly ickworthy, it bears truth. MAX is a space to connect, network, rant about the state of the creative industry, and, most importantly, a place to show up for your community.

It's no secret the creative industry was, and at times still is, a place of inequality. Be it race, gender, disability or age, while we have made strides to improve things, there are still gaps to be filled – something that Adobe is trying to address.

To learn more, I caught up with Karen Robinson, Vice President, Associate General Counsel, Litigation & Intellectual Property and leader of Adobe’s Black Employee Network, to discuss how Adobe is enacting change with purpose.

According to recent reports, I've been at the organization for about 14 years. BEN (Black Employee Network) started in the US, and I'm a founding member. Initially, it was an effort to build community, so we slowly started expanding. We had chapters in San Jose, San Francisco, Utah and Seattle, but then we started expanding internationally. Our largest community of Black Adobe employees is actually outside of the US, in the UK – BEN UK is a really strong presence.

I've been the executive sponsor for BEN for probably seven or eight years now, and it continues to be a focused effort that I'm really proud of. What's really interesting about BEN in particular is the allies. It's not just our Black employees – I love that there are so many people who get involved even when it's not necessarily part of their specific community.

In a recent development, it's about intersectionality. So, we have Access at Adobe, Asian/Pacific Islander at Adobe (APIA), Black Employee Network (BEN), Hispanic/Latinx at Adobe (HOLA), Indigenous/First Nations at Adobe (IFNA), Jewish Employee Network (JEN), Middle East/North Africa at Adobe (MENA), Pride at Adobe, Veterans Employee Network (VEN), and Women at Adobe. That's a really lovely thing about our Employee Networks in general, but I'm so proud of BEN. It's something that we put a lot of heart and effort into, and it sustains a lot of us.

We've always looked at inclusivity as something wildly crucial.

I'm responsible for some of our AI ethics and innovation, and as part of that, we made sure inclusivity is part of it. Looking at AI, how it can be used and what it's being trained on, if you're not focused on challenges of inclusivity, you're missing out on large communities. That means the tools you're creating aren't serving those communities, so they're not the best tools you can create.

Industry observers note that our Employee Networks all developed out of a community's desire to be represented – to reflect their culture and the things they found to be important – and reflect them in the Adobe culture. The company really leans into it. It's not just ticking a box, or even just about minority groups getting together to have a sense of community. It's a way to make sure that we're offering the best products that reflect the communities we're serving. It's about empowering creativity for everyone. How do you do that if you're not including everyone?

Sure. You can look at the numbers. I'm not saying anything that's shocking or outrageous. There is still opportunity for more inclusivity within the broader sort of industry.

Something I didn't realise was how much representation mattered. It wasn't until I got to a point where I had people coming up to me and saying, "Hey, I, I didn't even realise that someone like you could exist at a tech firm, it makes me think that there's room and opportunity and growth for me.".

For a long time, minority communities were being told, "You need to be in science or technology." The reality is, you don't. There are entire swaths of the industry you can be involved in and not have a science or math background, but they needed to hear that and see that. I don't have a technical degree, and yet here I am – the first Black SVP at Adobe.

I look at the numbers, and we're growing. Success breeds success, and representation is a huge part of that.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).
