#138373. Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1006 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility.
  • Recent findings suggest that the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol.
  • In a recent development, that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a new reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

Recent findings suggest that the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”.

In a recent development, that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”.

In a recent development, but is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Sources indicate that our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a big deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Industry observers note that beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Recent findings suggest that separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson says. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”.

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial complications that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”.

According to recent reports, as with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson states. It’s also extra vital to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

There’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she states—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Peter Hansen unless stated.

This year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, he selects five projects that showcase his work.

Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.

“My practice is centred around material culture, exploring the relationship between objects, meaning and everyday life,” Skinner told Dezeen.

“What connects my work is an interest in how forms carry associations and how these can be reshaped to offer new perspectives on things we know and take for granted.”.

Skinner finds that the things that excite him about design are also “the same things that make me suffer”.

“You never quite know what’s coming next when running your own practice, but there’s also something exciting about that uncertainty,” he said.

“A material or an object you’ve overlooked for years can suddenly become the starting point for a whole body of work.”.

Over the coming year, along with creating new collections and public installations, Skinner hopes to dedicate more time to research.

“I want to make more room for research and experimentation, and give myself time to follow an interest before knowing exactly where it might lead,” he noted.

Industry observers note that “When I started researching Afro combs at Konstfack, I became aware of how much history and symbolism an everyday tool can hold. That experience still informs how I work,” he continued.

“I want to keep exploring the objects and forms we take for granted, looking at the meanings they’ve inherited and what happens when you change their material, scale or context.”.

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning Skinner, as described by the designer:.

“An ongoing project in which vintage glass sourced from flea markets and second-hand shops is brought together in sculptural lighting compositions.

“Drawing on the memories and associations embedded in these found objects, the work explores the relationship between material, memory and light.”.

“Crafted in my studio, these combs celebrate rituals and traditions surrounding textured hair.

“Informed by historical references and personal experiences, they reimagine an everyday object through distinctive forms and symbols.”.

“Extending the exploration of beauty rituals within the Syntax collection, the Vanity Table offers an alternative reading of an object associated with personal grooming.”.

“These one-of-a-kind pieces, a daybed and an armchair, are upholstered in hand-dyed canvas in deep magenta hues.

“Combining traditional upholstery techniques with an experimental approach to colour and detail, the pieces embrace the irregularities of the dyeing process, making them an integral part of their character.”.

“This piece of furniture explores our relationship to the mechanical lock. The lock is integrated into the leg, with keys used to secure the connection between the leg and the seat.

“The keys can also serve as hooks for keychains and personal belongings, inviting individual expression.”.

Photography by Peter Hansen unless stated.

📅 05 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti.
  • Sources indicate that A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck.
  • Sources indicate that from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

Sources indicate that A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

Sources indicate that from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

It has been revealed that finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

Sources indicate that you can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

It has been revealed that communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

In a recent development, while generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any challenges.

Industry observers note that hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

Imagine checking into a Park Hyatt — marble floors, a sommelier who remembers your name by day two, a room that costs $400 a night — and knowing you paid for it with points you earned by writing your rent check. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee.

Most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock.

Recent findings suggest that once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Industry observers note that aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Sources indicate that did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar complications).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Sources indicate that thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

According to recent reports, peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

According to recent reports, the yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Recent findings suggest that blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Recent findings suggest that though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

In a recent development, ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That noted, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

Breaking: Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone.
  • It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body.
  • Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy fresh medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

Sources indicate that but retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

In a recent development, mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next substantial thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

Recent findings suggest that but retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” states Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”.

Sources indicate that the medication is presently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide owners lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

According to recent reports, “Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”.

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”.

Industry observers note that that includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

According to recent reports, but compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

It has been revealed that dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you initiative to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he indicates.

Industry observers note that but, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

According to recent reports, dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

Sources indicate that “Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle strategy focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel notes. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

It has been revealed that if you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali claims. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more notable, he points out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food.

That being mentioned, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:.

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:.

Sources indicate that L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

It has been revealed that in a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

According to recent reports, however, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.).

Sources indicate that and though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.).

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being mentioned, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:.

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Industry observers note that research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Peter Vinther (unless stated otherwise).
  • Sources indicate that architect and designer Patricia Urquiola has chosen fellow multidisciplinary Laerke Ryom as her pick for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler.
  • Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people’s attention as one of the co-founders of the design community Ukurant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Peter Vinther (unless stated otherwise).

Sources indicate that architect and designer Patricia Urquiola has chosen fellow multidisciplinary Laerke Ryom as her pick for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, Ryom discusses her innovative work and how it’s rooted in Danish design traditions.

Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people’s attention as one of the co-founders of the design community Ukurant.

Together with fellow founders Josefine Krabbe Munck, Kamma Rosa Schytte and Kasper Kyster, Ryom demonstrated her work as part of its first exhibition at Danish design week 3 Days of Design in 2020, and Ukurant promptly became a recurring highlight of the design event.

Since graduating from the Royal Academy of Fine Art in Copenhagen’s master’s program in furniture and object in 2022, Ryom’s tactile designs have continued to evolve, and she has worked with a range of materials and products.

For her collection Blå, she made handwoven denim upholstery out of worn-out jeans, while the Buckle chair, made with furniture brand Fredericia, resembles a leather jacket.

“I find very interesting the way she moves naturally between furniture and textiles, starting from discarded materials and giving them a new logic through simple gestures,” Urquiola mentioned of why she chose Ryom.

“There is something light in the way she works. Her work feels open and still very much in evolution.”.

This experimentation has become something of a signature for Ryom, whose latest exhibition, Raiments, was a sleek exploration of how upholstery could almost become a furniture piece in itself.

To the designer, her work now is in some ways a continuation of the projects she worked on during her time at the Royal Academy.

“During my studies, I was investigating different materials and different typologies, which I actually still think I’m kind of doing – I don’t see myself as limited to one material,” Ryom told Dezeen.

While she “really strongly identifies as a furniture designer”, Ryom has also designed smaller products, such as metal bowls for the Bread & Butter exhibition in Copenhagen and quilted lamps.

To her, function is always at the forefront, and Ryom believes that even details that appear to be purely decorative have a function if they tell a story.

“Even when I’m doing collectible things for galleries, I’m always thinking of the functionality of the pieces,” she explained.

“Even if you can say, ‘[what’s functional] about doing a little skirt on a chair’, as on the Raiments chair, it tells a story; a story of the cover being loose, something that is its own thing, [separate] from the frame. For me, that’s still a function or a means to an end.”.

Her aim is to create pieces that straddle the line between collectible and functional design; something that is artistic and yet commercial enough to someday go into production.

“I want it to be something where the distance between the categories disappears, and they become a shared thing,” Ryom explained.

“That’s something I think a lot about, that the collectible design and the artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production.”.

The collectible design and artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production.

The idea of giving beauty to everyday objects, rather than creating pieces that are purely functional or purely aesthetic, is one that has deep roots in the Scandinavian design tradition.

While Ryom’s pieces might not be the pale-wood designs usually associated with Danish design – though she has worked in wood, using offcut wooden pieces to design furniture for Ukurant in 2023 – she sees herself as part of this tradition.

“Even if people don’t think that what I do looks like typical Danish design, I feel like it’s completely rooted and very fundamentally based on the principles of the Danish design tradition,” she explained.

“I view myself as someone who is not in opposition, but who is developing or following along [with it].”.

While her own pieces in the past have so far mostly been made in smaller quantities, Ryom sees positively on the current trend of big brands, such as IKEA and Disney, working with younger designers and mass-producing their work.

She believes it helps to spread knowledge about designers to a public that isn’t always aware of the people behind the products.

“I think it’s an important thing because what we see, at least here in Denmark, is that the knowledge about designers today, for the general public, is crazy small for a nation that kind of brands itself as a design nation,” Ryom remarked.

“Talking to my parents, even with them having a designer for a daughter, they’re still trying to figure out ‘what is it that you actually do’?

Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it.

Ryom herself, meanwhile, says she sees a big difference between her current work and that of a few years ago. She thinks it comes from “starting to believe in yourself and your intuition, and getting more skilled in your craft”.

But, she also consciously works on developing her ideas and taking them from the initial inspiration stage to the final product.

“Inspiration is something that I stumble upon in my everyday life, but at the same time, it only becomes interesting when I sit down and work with it,” she mentioned.

“Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it and investigate what the substance of the inspiration actually is.”.

As someone who’s constantly exploring latest materials and ways of designing, Ryom also highlights the importance of collaboration. She says that while she likes doing a lot of the work on her furniture herself, she has also gotten better at reaching out to experts to get input for some of her pieces, including her Enfold chair.

The steel chair is covered in a ruched leather upholstery, held in place by buttons, that creates a very tactile, sculptural seat.

“It did it all myself, but I reached out to a fashion designer who does a lot of leather bags, and I could talk to her and ask ‘how would you do the finishing here, or what kind of tool would you use there?'” she said.“I really like figuring things out myself and doing it myself, but seeking the knowledge of those people who have really done the craft.”.

Being chosen by Urquiola meant a lot to Ryom, who really admires the Spanish designer.

“It was actually a little surreal, because she is someone that I look up to,” Ryom said. “When you can say anyone in the world, I feel very, very honoured that she pointed at me – that’s a huge thing.”.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

Sources indicate that inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or problems with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any problems.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

Recent findings suggest that if your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

It has been revealed that for some latest parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:.

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

This stop-motion horror game proves there's something deeply unsettling about handmade art

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stop-motion animation has been a popular aesthetic in indie games, giving creations a more tactile, handcrafted, and personal touch.
  • Industry observers note that "From studying art, I had just so much more affinity for tangible things and seeing what the materials give me as I'm making things," he tells me.
  • While Talha & Jack Co's previous two games, the Scottish pagan action-adventure Judero and the chill post-apocalyptic robot-mining adventure Mashina, were sprite-based, Abide is more ambitious: a first-person 3D game, so they're scanning the epoxy clay models with photogrammetry, though cutscenes are still being created as stop-motion animation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stop-motion animation has been a popular aesthetic in indie games, giving creations a more tactile, handcrafted, and personal touch. But while many developers simply emulate this style digitally, two-person indie studio Talha and Jack Co prides itself on making real physical models. For co-founder Jack King-Spooner, creative director of the upcoming game Abide, it's always been what matters most.

Industry observers note that "From studying art, I had just so much more affinity for tangible things and seeing what the materials give me as I'm making things," he tells me. "From my first game 15 years ago, I've always been invested in tangible assets. I couldn't really be bothered drawing pixel art when I could just make a little model and then photograph it from different angles, move it a little bit. It was just so much quicker for me.".

While Talha & Jack Co's previous two games, the Scottish pagan action-adventure Judero and the chill post-apocalyptic robot-mining adventure Mashina, were sprite-based, Abide is more ambitious: a first-person 3D game, so they're scanning the epoxy clay models with photogrammetry, though cutscenes are still being created as stop-motion animation.

"The models are much, much bigger; they've got so much more detail," King-Spooner states, while bringing up a model in his hand as close up to the camera during our video call so that I can see the latex allowing for very realistic textures of skin pores and lips. "I'm always pushing myself with techniques, and finding new ways to do things. A lot of artists become frozen and immobilised with their craft because they think that there's a right way of doing things, whereas I just like doing things however I can.".

It has been revealed that some of that detail nonetheless does have to be reduced, as a larger, more detailed model could be the equivalent of a super high-res model with 500,000 polygons. "We cut down to like 6,000 polygons so that we can hit good frame rates. They're a bit chunky, but for me they only needed to be recognisable as the same character as in the stop-motion cutscenes. I know lots of people love really tight graphics, but I'd rather spend the time on engaging story and engaging gameplay.".

Sources indicate that there are also additional parts that are made for the stop-motion cutscenes. For example, in a scene that requires a close-up of a character washing their hands, they use a larger hand for that shot instead of zooming in on the model's hands, then cut back to the normal model (something Thunderbirds' Jerry Anderson was famous for).

Even with games like Judero, the devs have noted that their stop-motion style has an inherent creepiness, so given that Abide is an "extreme stop motion horror" that includes prosthetic gore effects, King-Spooner is relishing that by doubling down on it. "There's something very abject and horrific about stop motion animation," he says, "It's got this nostalgia, but it's also got this kind of uncanny movement to it which you project life onto.".

To an extent, it also feels like a deliberate response to counter the cosy perceptions people might have of this aesthetic. "A lot of handcrafted games are a bit kind of soft, aren't they? I think with Abide it's really nice that people will think, 'Oh god, a real person, this guy Jack is a real monstrous kind of person that he's made such perverted little dolls doing such horrible things!' I think it adds to the tangibility that it's very much a person's handiwork.".

It nonetheless has an idyllic setting on the surface, set in the St Boniface retreat in the secluded countryside with a group of eight residents from different walks of life in some kind of need of them; at night it descends into full-on horror as you start sneaking around and explore parts of the house you probably shouldn't.

"One aspect which is very disturbing is they're all somehow reflections of myself," King-Spooner admits. "I think it's notable for a creator to recognise that the work you output is somehow autobiographical of yourself. I'm just rather kind of transparent about it.".

In many environments, King-Spooner has also opted to build physical sets or paint textures, such as splattering red paint to make wood textures look bloody or putting on muddy boots and trampling them on white paper to scan.

According to recent reports, if there's a downside to creating physical models and objects, it's that there's often no room to keep them, so after production is over, everything is either chucked out or the clay is mushed up to be reused, although King-Spooner isn't especially precious about preservation. As he bluntly puts it, "We're all going to be dirt in the ground.".

Abide is coming soon to PC, and you can wishlist it on Steam.

#138357. Tech Report: Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

📅 31 Jul 2024 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (654 w)

Tech Report: Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

📅 31 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 3 min read (654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people.
  • But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne?
  • According to recent reports, salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”.

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

According to recent reports, salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

It has been revealed that adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Industry observers note that salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more swiftly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

In a recent development, so… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

In a recent development, which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Industry observers note that adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Industry observers note that adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Sources indicate that research highlights that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

In a recent development, though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Recent findings suggest that feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation.
  • The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

“These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

The research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers discovered that while participants stated they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

In a recent development, “We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh notes. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”.

Industry observers note that people are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

Sources indicate that as a result, Dr. Gallagher indicates she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”.

In a recent development, these chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

“Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen claims. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Recent findings suggest that loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a significant impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen indicates.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan notes. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

According to recent reports, of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan says. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”.

Ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she says. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”.

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

According to recent reports, thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

According to recent reports, drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

According to recent reports, when you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Preparing for a Thai massage is simple!

In a recent development, pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Photography by Fran Mart.

London architecture practice Tuckey Design Studio has renovated and extended Bay House in rural Yorkshire, using a rich, moody palette intended to evoke the feeling of a wine bar.

The project involved reconfiguring and expanding the country house dating from the early 2000s, while introducing a garden spa and sauna.

Tuckey Design Studio was tasked by the clients to recreate the feeling of their favourite wine bar, which informed a palette of dark timber carpentry, terracotta-painted walls and a bespoke wine storage cabinet alongside a tasting area.

“The ambition was clear from the beginning: to bring the atmosphere of a much-loved London wine bar into the home,” project lead Fraser Biggins told Dezeen.

“The clients’ enthusiasm for wine and music became vital touchstones for the design, informing both the arrangement of the spaces and the character of the interiors,” he added.

The home’s previously cramped interiors are now centred on a large, double-height atrium, which serves as both a point of arrival and a gathering and tasting space with a bespoke timber “wine wall”.

This hall is finished with dark timber panelling, terrazzo floors and terracotta paintwork, with a wall alongside an arched composite stone staircase punctured by small square openings.

This central space leads through into the social spaces, with a kitchen and dining space finished using similar dark timber panelling and concrete countertops.

Recent findings suggest that the stairs lead up to the first floor via a landing with a built-in bench, where a balcony connecting the bedrooms enjoys views of the hall below. It also looks across the garden through windows in a newly introduced bay window extension.

“The central hall forms the organising principle of the house, providing a shared space from which the surrounding family rooms and activities unfold,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“A series of interconnected spaces, galleries and overlooking balconies create visual connections across different levels, allowing the house to feel both connected and varied,” he added.

On the first floor, two of the existing bedrooms have been converted into a games room and bar space, finished in dark shades of green and grey.

Alongside them are four ensuite bedrooms finished in warmer shades of pale pink and yellow, with each featuring a hand-painted mural designed to “reflect the character of each occupant”.

“Material choices were guided by a desire for honesty, durability and longevity,” Biggins told Dezeen.

“We wanted the spaces to feel timeless and comfortable, without relying too heavily on traditional materials or references.”.

“Instead, the palette brings together robust, tactile finishes that feel natural and lived-in, allowing the character of the materials to speak for themselves,” he added.

The exterior of the extension has been finished in composite stone and dark accoya wood, and looks across the home’s garden to the standalone spa and sauna, which was designed as a “complementary counterpoint” to the main home.

Previous projects by Tuckey Design Studio include a home in Wiltshire constructed using walls of unstabilised rammed earth and a residence within a converted chapel in Devon.

#138351. Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity.
  • Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.
  • At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

Recent findings suggest that “Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

Sources indicate that they also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik says.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

Running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

Incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik indicates. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”.

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

Industry observers note that “Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik says. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

The steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”.

Still, it’s vital to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she notes.

In fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik claims.

Both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

If you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik says. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

In a recent development, but if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik says.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s notable to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

In a recent development, “Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik says. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”.

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

Ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.
